title: Israel's coalition test, human-cell mice and the EV surge

stories.headline: Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot gets first chance to form Israel's government
stories.headlineZh: 内塔尼亚胡劲敌艾森科特获授权组建以色列新政府
stories.summaryZh: 67名议员推荐艾森科特，他须在28天内组建联合政府，阿拉伯政党的角色成最大争议。
stories.c1:
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has given Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who leads the Yashar party, the first opportunity to form a new government, dealing a significant blow to his rival Benjamin Netanyahu. After taking the weekend for deliberation, Herzog's office said factions representing 67 members of the Knesset had recommended Eisenkot, compared with 46 who backed Netanyahu, the leader of Likud. One faction with seven members chose not to endorse anyone.

Eisenkot now has 28 days to assemble a coalition, a period the president may extend by a further 14 days if negotiations are still under way. Should he fail, Herzog could turn to Netanyahu instead, and if the deadlock drags on, Israelis may find themselves heading back to the polls in the new year.

Securing a workable majority will be far from straightforward. Arab-Israeli parties will hold a record 19 seats in the incoming parliament, and their role has become the main sticking point. Avigdor Liberman, who leads Yisrael Beiteinu, has ruled out sitting in any government that includes them. Without those parties, Eisenkot would need backing from the ultra-Orthodox factions of Netanyahu's former coalition, yet he campaigned on forcing ultra-Orthodox men to complete compulsory military service. Their exemptions were struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024.

Meanwhile, Likud and other right-wing parties have accused their opponents of stealing the election and have alleged foreign interference. Police and the Shin Bet are investigating claims that foreign money was used to boost turnout in Arab-Israeli communities, although the head of the elections committee said the concerns were not serious enough to undermine the vote's integrity. Netanyahu, who has not been seen in public since polling day, has called for a unity government, an idea Herzog had already rejected.
stories.b2:
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has chosen Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a new government. Eisenkot is a former head of the military, the leader of the Yashar party and a rival of Benjamin Netanyahu. Parties with 67 members of parliament recommended Eisenkot, while parties with 46 members supported Netanyahu.

Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition. The president can give him 14 more days if talks are continuing. If he does not succeed, Herzog can ask Netanyahu to try. If nobody can form a government, there could be another election next year.

The task will be difficult. Arab-Israeli parties will have a record 19 seats, and this is the biggest problem. Avigdor Liberman, the leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, says he will not join a government that includes them. Without them, Eisenkot would need help from ultra-Orthodox parties. However, he wants ultra-Orthodox men to do military service, which those parties oppose.

Likud and other right-wing parties claim the election was stolen and say there was foreign interference. Police are investigating claims about foreign money, but the head of the elections committee says the result is still valid. Netanyahu has asked for a unity government, but Herzog has already said no.

stories.headline: Human brain tissue grown inside mice could help study brain disorders
stories.headlineZh: 人类脑组织在小鼠体内生长，助力脑疾病研究
stories.summaryZh: 斯坦福团队将人类脑类器官植入缺失大脑皮层的小鼠，组织约占脑容量一半，引发伦理讨论。
stories.c1:
Scientists at Stanford University have grown human brain tissue inside living mice, an achievement they hope will shed new light on conditions such as schizophrenia, cerebral palsy and dementia. The study, published in Nature and led by psychiatry professor Sergiu Pasca, set out to tackle a long-standing problem: ethical and safety constraints make living human brain tissue extremely difficult to study.

The team genetically engineered mice to develop without most of their cerebral cortex and hippocampus, regions involved in movement, learning and memory. When the animals were two days old, researchers implanted organoids, lab-grown clusters of roughly 100,000 cells derived from donors' stem cells. The procedure succeeded in 25 of 29 mice. Within three months, the human tissue had grown about fivefold, tapped into the animals' blood supply and accounted for around half of their brain volume.

Strikingly, the mice walked and vocalised more or less normally, and in maze tests they outperformed mice lacking the human tissue, suggesting it contributed to cognition. Some cells even developed into von Economo neurons, rare cells found in highly social species such as humans, apes, whales and elephants. When deprived of oxygen, the mice showed brain damage and poor limb coordination, offering a possible model for cerebral palsy, which rodents seldom develop naturally.

Unsurprisingly, the work raises thorny ethical questions. The researchers stress that this is not a brain transplant and that the animals do not think like humans; they also halted the experiments before any signs of consciousness appeared. John Evans, a sociologist who was not involved, argued that the study itself does not raise major ethical problems, but cautioned that the field lacks clear stopping points on the path towards primates. Calls for firmer oversight of organoid research are growing.
stories.b2:
Researchers at Stanford University have grown human brain tissue inside living mice. They hope this will help scientists understand illnesses such as schizophrenia, cerebral palsy and dementia. The study was published in the journal Nature. Living human brain tissue is very hard to study for ethical and safety reasons.

The scientists changed the genes of mice so that they grew without most of the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. When the mice were two days old, the team added organoids, which are small groups of human cells grown in a lab. This worked in 25 of 29 mice. After three months, the human tissue made up about half of each mouse's brain.

The mice could walk and make sounds fairly normally. In maze tests, they did better than mice without human tissue. Some human cells also became rare von Economo neurons, which are found in very social animals such as humans and whales. The mice could also help scientists study cerebral palsy.

The research raises ethical questions. The scientists say the mice do not think like humans, and they stopped the experiments before any signs of consciousness. Some experts want clearer rules for this kind of research.

stories.headline: Iran war fuel shock speeds up the global switch to electric cars
stories.headlineZh: 伊朗战争引发油价冲击，加速全球电动车转型
stories.summaryZh: 油价飙升推动电动车销量大增，澳大利亚纯电车销量连续两月超过汽油车。
stories.c1:
During the 1979 oil crisis, US president Jimmy Carter stood beside a solar hot water system at the White House and urged Americans to embrace clean energy. Experts now suggest another conflict involving Iran could prove a tipping point in the move away from fossil fuels. Since the US and Israel began bombing Iran in February, fuel prices have soared and sales of electric vehicles have risen sharply around the world.

Australia is a case in point. EVs now make up close to a quarter of new car sales, and in September and October battery electric cars outsold petrol models. Sales have reached record levels in Europe, hitting 37 per cent in Germany in October, while demand is gathering pace across South-East Asia, and Laos suspended imports of combustion-engine cars in May. One energy expert even described Donald Trump as the world's best salesperson for EVs. Ironically, the US is the only country where EV sales have fallen.

The economic argument is also becoming harder to dismiss. Before the crisis, the world was on track to spend about US$4 trillion a year on oil and gas, and one coalition forecasts that this year's bill could exceed US$5 trillion. By comparison, a net-zero energy transition is estimated to cost roughly US$3.5 trillion annually. An Ember report found that the world's electric cars saved around US$20 billion in crude oil costs in the six months after the war began.

Even so, the shift still has a long way to go. EVs account for only about 5 per cent of cars on the road, and coal, oil and gas still supply around 60 per cent of the world's final energy. With COP31 taking place this week and electrification high on the agenda, the question is whether governments will seize the moment.
stories.b2:
In 1979, during an oil crisis, US president Jimmy Carter asked Americans to use more solar energy. Now experts say a new war involving Iran could be a turning point in the move away from fossil fuels. Since the US and Israel started bombing Iran in February, fuel prices have gone up and people are buying electric cars.

In Australia, electric vehicles are now almost a quarter of new car sales. In September and October, more battery electric cars were sold than petrol cars. EV sales are also at record levels in Europe, and they are growing in South-East Asia. However, in the US, EV sales have actually fallen.

Money is a big part of the story. Before the war, the world was spending about US$4 trillion a year on oil and gas. This year, the cost could be more than US$5 trillion. Moving to net-zero energy would cost about US$3.5 trillion a year. Electric cars around the world saved about US$20 billion in oil in the first six months of the war.

But the change is not finished. Only about 5 per cent of cars on the road are electric, and fossil fuels still provide about 60 per cent of the world's final energy. The COP31 climate talks are taking place this week, and electrification is an important topic.

stories.headline: Experts warn Victoria's crowded prisons face pressure from tough election promises
stories.headlineZh: 专家警告：维州监狱拥挤，选举中的强硬承诺将加剧压力
stories.summaryZh: 维州监狱已达92%容量，两大党都主张严打犯罪，但都未说明新增监狱成本。
stories.c1:
With Victorians heading to the polls on 28 November, experts are warning that the state's prisons may struggle to cope with the tough-on-crime promises of both major parties. At the start of November, Victoria's prisons were operating at 92 per cent capacity, holding 4,624 sentenced prisoners and 3,268 people on remand.

Premier Ben Carroll is introducing tougher laws, while the Coalition under Jess Wilson has pledged a firmer approach, including 1,500 extra police recruits on top of the 1,500 Labor is seeking. Building prisons, however, does not come cheap: the maximum-security Western Plains prison near Lara cost $1.19 billion. Neither party directly answered questions about the additional cost of more prison space and corrections officers. Labor points to more than 1,200 extra beds and 1,200 extra officers it has already delivered, while Shadow Corrections Minister Brad Battin says a Coalition government would manage numbers within existing facilities.

Arie Freiberg, a former chair of the Sentencing Advisory Council, warned that more police and stricter rules would put pressure on prisons and could mean more people being held in police cells. "Justice is not cheap," he said, arguing that investing in services for people with mental illness or drug and alcohol problems would be more cost-effective than locking them up.

Not everyone shares that view. Swinburne law professor Mirko Bagaric blames lenient sentencing under Labor for the rise in crime and regards new prisons as a worthwhile investment, provided they focus on violent and sexual offenders. Notably, Victoria's prison population fell from 8,102 to 5,915 between 2019 and 2025, even as the crime rate rose, a statistic that is likely to fuel debate on both sides.
stories.b2:
Victorians will vote in a state election on 28 November. Experts say the state's prisons may not be able to handle the tougher crime policies of both major parties. In early November, Victoria's prisons were at 92 per cent capacity.

Premier Ben Carroll is bringing in tougher laws. The Coalition, led by Jess Wilson, also promises a tougher approach and 1,500 more police recruits. But prisons are very expensive. The Western Plains prison near Lara cost $1.19 billion. Neither party clearly explained how it would pay for more prison space and staff. Labor says it has already added more than 1,200 beds and 1,200 officers.

Arie Freiberg, who used to lead the Sentencing Advisory Council, says more police and stricter rules will put more pressure on prisons. He believes spending money on mental health and drug and alcohol services is better value than prisons.

Law professor Mirko Bagaric disagrees. He says light sentences have led to more crime, and he thinks new prisons are a good investment if they are used for violent and sexual offenders. Between 2019 and 2025, the number of prisoners in Victoria fell, but the crime rate went up.

vocab.en: to find it very hard to deal with a situation or demand
vocab.example: Hospitals are struggling to cope with the winter flu season.

vocab.en: favouring strict laws and harsh punishments for crime
vocab.example: The candidate ran a tough-on-crime campaign in the outer suburbs.

vocab.en: to make a formal promise to do or give something

vocab.en: to be expensive

vocab.en: to cause difficulties or strain for a system or person

vocab.en: giving good results for the money spent
vocab.example: Insulating your roof is a cost-effective way to cut energy bills.

vocab.en: less strict or severe than expected
vocab.example: Some parents think the school is too lenient about phones in class.

vocab.en: worth the time, money or effort spent
vocab.example: Volunteering at the shelter was a really worthwhile experience.

questions.explain: 原文：prisons were operating at 92 per cent capacity，并未满员，故为False。

questions.q: Mirko Bagaric has advised the Coalition on its justice policy.
questions.explain: 文中只介绍了 Bagaric 的观点，没有提到他是否为联盟党提供建议，故为Not Given。

questions.q: Freiberg thinks funding mental health and addiction services is better value than imprisonment.
questions.explain: 原文：investing in services for people with mental illness or drug and alcohol problems would be more cost-effective than locking them up，故为True。

questions.q: What happened to Victoria's prison population between 2019 and 2025?
options: It rose along with the crime rate
It doubled because of tougher laws
It fell while the crime rate rose
questions.explain: 原文：prison population fell from 8,102 to 5,915 ... even as the crime rate rose。

stories.discuss: Is building more prisons the best way to make communities safer, or should money go elsewhere? Why?

dialogue.title: Catching Up Over Coffee
dialogue.setting: Two old uni friends meet at a café on Lygon Street on Monday morning and end up chatting about the news.
dialogue.settingZh: 周一早上，两位大学老友在莱贡街的一家咖啡馆见面，聊起了新闻。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Sorry I'm late — the tram was crawling the whole way down Swanston.
lines.zh: 抱歉我迟到了——电车一路在斯旺斯顿街上慢吞吞地爬。

lines.name: Callum
lines.en: No worries, I've only just ordered. Flat white for you, as usual?
lines.zh: 没关系，我也刚点完。还是老样子，给你来杯馥芮白？

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: You know me too well. So, what's new? Still thinking about getting a car?
lines.zh: 你太了解我了。最近怎么样？还在考虑买车吗？

lines.name: Callum
lines.en: Yeah, and with petrol prices through the roof, I'm leaning towards an EV.
lines.zh: 是啊，油价贵得离谱，我比较倾向买电动车。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Makes sense. Apparently they outsold petrol cars here for the last two months.
lines.zh: 有道理。听说过去两个月电动车的销量都超过汽油车了。

lines.name: Callum
lines.en: Really? That's wild. Mind you, I'd still have to sort out charging at my flat.
lines.zh: 真的吗？太夸张了。不过话说回来，我还得解决公寓的充电问题。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Fair point. Did you see that story about mice with human brain cells?
lines.zh: 说得对。你看到那条关于小鼠体内有人类脑细胞的新闻了吗？

lines.name: Callum
lines.en: I did! Honestly, it's fascinating, but it also gives me the creeps a bit.
lines.zh: 看到了！说实话，挺神奇的，但也让我有点发毛。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Same. I get why they're doing it, but where do you draw the line?
lines.zh: 我也是。我理解他们为什么这么做，但界限该划在哪里呢？

lines.name: Callum
lines.en: Exactly. Anyway, are you across the state election? It's only a few weeks off.
lines.zh: 没错。对了，你关注州选举了吗？只剩几周了。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Sort of. Both sides keep banging on about crime, but nobody mentions the cost.
lines.zh: 算是吧。两边都一直在念叨犯罪问题，却没人提成本。

lines.name: Callum
lines.en: Typical. I reckon I'll just read the policies properly before I make up my mind.
lines.zh: 老一套了。我想还是先认真看看政策再做决定吧。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Good on you. Right, coffee's here — let's talk about something less heavy!
lines.zh: 你真靠谱。好了，咖啡来了——咱们聊点轻松的吧！
